definition: A mixture of hydrocarbons formed from ancient marine organisms buried by sediment and transformed by heat and pressure over millions of years. Finite and non-renewable.
msAccepts: formed from ancient biomass under heat and pressure
msAvoids: calling it a single compound or pure substance
saying it will be replaced within a human timescale

definition: A compound containing carbon and hydrogen only. The word only is load-bearing: any third element, such as the oxygen in ethanol, disqualifies the compound.
msAccepts: compound of carbon and hydrogen only
made of just carbon and hydrogen
msAvoids: saying contains carbon and hydrogen without 'only'

definition: Coal, natural gas and fuels derived from crude oil — fuels that come from things that were once alive, which is why the supply is finite.
msAccepts: finite because formation takes millions of years

definition: Describes a resource that cannot be replaced once used, or not for millions of years. Crude oil is non-renewable because formation vastly outpaces consumption.
msAccepts: cannot be replaced as quickly as it is used
msAvoids: saying it never regenerates at all without the timescale

definition: Forces of attraction between neighbouring molecules. They strengthen as molecules get bigger, which is why larger hydrocarbons boil higher, evaporate more slowly and flow less easily.
msAccepts: stronger intermolecular forces in larger molecules
more energy needed to overcome them
msAvoids: confusing them with covalent bonds inside molecules

definition: Describes a liquid that turns to a vapour easily at room temperature — it evaporates quickly. Volatility falls as hydrocarbon molecule size increases.
msAccepts: low boiling point liquids are volatile
msAvoids: confusing volatile with flammable or explosive

definition: A measure of how reluctantly a liquid flows. Viscosity rises with hydrocarbon molecule size because stronger attractions between molecules resist them sliding past each other.
msAccepts: how thick or runny a liquid is
larger molecules give more viscous liquids

definition: The temperature at which a liquid boils — the same temperature at which the gas condenses back to liquid, so it can also be called the condensation point.
msAccepts: temperature at which a liquid becomes a gas

definition: A mixture of hydrocarbons with a narrow range of chain lengths and similar boiling points, separated from crude oil in the fractionating column. Every fraction is still a mixture.
msAccepts: mixture of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points
separated from crude oil by distillation
msAvoids: calling a fraction a pure compound

definition: The industrial separation of crude oil into fractions: heated vapours rise up a column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top, and each fraction condenses at the height matching its boiling point.
msAccepts: vapours rise, condense at different heights
column hot at bottom, cool at top
msAvoids: describing it as a chemical reaction
confusing it with simple distillation of a pure liquid

definition: The tall tower used in oil refineries, hot at the bottom and progressively cooler towards the top, where rising hydrocarbon vapours condense at different heights according to their boiling points.
msAccepts: hot at the bottom, cooler at the top
condensation height set by boiling point
msAvoids: saying it filters by size mechanically
placing the cooler end at the bottom

definition: The very large hydrocarbons whose boiling points exceed the column temperature: they never vaporise and drain from the base of the column as a thick liquid, the source of bitumen.
msAccepts: very large molecules that do not vaporise
collected at the bottom of the column
msAvoids: calling residue a waste product with no use
saying it condenses from gas high up

definition: The smallest fraction: methane, ethane, propane and butane, which never condense in the column and leave the top as gases. Bottled as liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for domestic heating and cooking.
msAccepts: gases leaving the top of the column
used as LPG for heating and cooking
msAvoids: listing large molecules in the fraction
confusing LPG with natural gas alone

definition: The petrol fraction: a mixture of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points in the middle-small size range, used as fuel for cars. Octane is one of its components.
msAvoids: assigning it to ships or furnaces

definition: The fraction used as jet-aircraft fuel, as domestic heating oil, and — under the old name paraffin — for small heaters and lamps.
The fraction used as fuel for buses, lorries, some cars and some railway engines. Some diesel is also cracked into more useful products including petrol.
msAccepts: used in some cars and trains
can be cracked to smaller molecules

definition: The thick fraction burned in ships' boilers and for industrial heating, where slow burning of large molecules is an advantage rather than a problem.
msAvoids: omitting the marine and industrial uses
confusing it with bitumen's non-fuel use

definition: A thick, black material from the bottom of the column, melted and mixed with small pieces of rock to make the top surface of roads. Its molecules are too large to be worth burning.
msAvoids: saying it condenses at the top of the column

definition: A substance that, when burned, releases heat energy. The definition names two claims only — burning happens and heat is released — and does not require the fuel to be a hydrocarbon.
msAccepts: substance burned as an energy source
msAvoids: defining fuel as something that contains hydrocarbons
saying fuels must produce carbon dioxide

definition: Burning in plenty of oxygen. Hydrocarbons burn completely to carbon dioxide and water only, releasing a large amount of heat.
msAvoids: listing carbon monoxide among complete-combustion products
saying limited oxygen still gives complete combustion

definition: Burning with insufficient oxygen. Products include toxic carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) as well as water — the carbon cannot be fully oxidised to carbon dioxide.
msAvoids: listing carbon dioxide as the only carbon product
saying the fuel is different rather than the oxygen supply

definition: A colourless, odourless, toxic gas from incomplete combustion. It is poisonous because it reduces the ability of the blood to carry oxygen around the body.
msAvoids: saying it is poisonous because it is acidic
claiming it has a warning smell

definition: A gas that traps heat radiated from the Earth's surface — heat that originally came from the Sun. Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels is the main example in this chapter.
msAccepts: carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas
msAvoids: saying greenhouse gases create heat themselves
confusing the greenhouse effect with acid rain

definition: SO₂, formed when the sulfur impurities in fossil fuels burn: S + O₂ → SO₂. Converted in the atmosphere to sulfuric acid, it is a major cause of acid rain.
msAvoids: saying sulfur is part of the hydrocarbon molecules
confusing it with the oxides of nitrogen source

definition: Gases such as NO and NO₂, grouped as NOₓ. Formed when engine temperatures are high enough to make nitrogen and oxygen from the air react; converted to nitric acid, they contribute to acid rain.
msAccepts: NO and NO2, general formula NOx
formed from N2 and O2 in the air at high temperature
contribute to acid rain via nitric acid
msAvoids: saying nitrogen comes from the fuel
confusing them with the sulfur impurity source

definition: Rain with a pH lower than the natural value of about 5.6 — often about pH 4 — because dissolved sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen form sulfuric and nitric acid in the atmosphere.
msAccepts: sulfuric and nitric acids dissolved in rain
damages trees, lakes, limestone buildings and iron
msAvoids: calling naturally acidic rain acid rain

definition: The process that converts long-chain alkanes into alkenes and shorter-chain alkanes: the fraction is vaporised and passed over a silica/alumina catalyst at about 600–700 °C.
msAccepts: long chains split into shorter alkanes and alkenes

definition: Breaking a substance into smaller molecules by heating. Cracking is thermal decomposition: heat supplies the energy, and no oxygen is involved.
msAccepts: one substance breaks into smaller ones on heating

definition: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up. In cracking, silica (silicon dioxide) and alumina (aluminium oxide) catalyse the splitting of long-chain alkanes.
msAccepts: speeds up reaction without being consumed
msAvoids: saying the catalyst is used up

definition: A saturated hydrocarbon: its carbon atoms are joined by single bonds only, so each carbon carries the maximum possible hydrogen. Cracking consumes long-chain alkanes.

An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C). Cracking always produces alkenes alongside shorter alkanes, and their reactivity makes them key industrial building blocks.
msAvoids: confusing the double bond with a ring
